t: Check if All Characters Have Equal Number of Occurrences -- Comparing Character Frequencies
o: A string is good when every distinct character in it occurs the same number of times; characters absent from the string are ignored entirely. For s = "abacbc" the counts are a:2, b:2, c:2, so all present characters share frequency 2 and the answer is true. For s = "aaabb" the counts are a:3 and b:2 -- the frequencies differ, so the answer is false. With n <= 1000 and only lowercase English letters, counting occurrences and comparing the resulting frequencies fits easily in linear time; no technique fancier than a frequency table is required.
k: The answer depends only on the multiset of character frequencies: build a frequency table and check that all of its values are equal.
Characters with zero occurrences are irrelevant -- only frequencies of characters actually present in s matter.
There are at most 26 lowercase letters, so counting needs only constant extra space with a fixed-size array.

a.n: Approach 1: Frequency Map Plus Set of Counts
a.i: Count how many times each character appears using a hash map, then collect all frequency values into a set. The string is good exactly when that set holds a single value, meaning every present character has the same frequency.
s: Count occurrences of every character with a hash map.
Insert all frequency values into a set.
Return whether the set contains exactly one value.
a.t: O(n) -- one pass to count plus a scan over at most 26 distinct characters
a.sp: O(1) -- the map never holds more than 26 entries

a.n: Approach 2: Fixed-Size Array With Early Exit
a.i: Because s contains only lowercase letters, a length-26 counter array removes hashing overhead entirely. After tallying, remember the first nonzero count seen and require every subsequent nonzero count to match it, which can bail out early instead of building a second structure.
s: Allocate a 26-slot counter array and tally each character.
Take the first nonzero count as the target frequency.
Scan the remaining slots: any nonzero count differing from the target returns false; otherwise return true.
a.t: O(n) -- a single counting pass plus a constant 26-slot verification
a.sp: O(1) -- one fixed array of 26 integers

w: Either approach passes comfortably; in an interview the hash-map version is fastest to explain, then mention the 26-letter optimization. Pitfalls: ignore zero counts (absent characters) and note a single-character string is trivially good. Useful follow-ups: allowing uppercase or Unicode forces the array back to a hash map, and variants like "equal frequencies after removing at most one character" reuse the same counting base.
